subject: Government
title: Rule of Law, Separation of Powers, and Human Rights
outline: Meaning and principles of the rule of law
Conditions for and limitations on the rule of law
Separation of powers: meaning and purpose
Fundamental human rights in the 1999 Constitution

modules.title: The Rule of Law
modules.html:
The rule of law means the supremacy of law over all persons and authorities: no one is above the law, and government itself must act within the law. The doctrine was systematised by A. V. Dicey in An Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution (1885) under three pillars:

  1. Supremacy of the law — no person may be punished except for a definite breach of law established in an ordinary court; there is no arbitrary or discretionary punishment.
  2. Equality before the law — all persons, including public officials, are subject to the same law administered by the same courts.
  3. The constitution as a consequence of individual rights — in Britain, rights derive from decisions of the courts in actual cases rather than from a written declaration.

Conditions necessary for the rule of law: an independent judiciary; a free press; an enlightened citizenry; democratic government; separation of powers; a well-trained and disciplined police force; and legal aid so that the poor can enforce their rights.

Limitations in practice: diplomatic immunity; immunity of the President, Vice-President, Governors and their deputies under section 308; parliamentary privileges; delegated legislation and administrative tribunals; states of emergency; detention under security legislation; the cost and delay of litigation; and, historically, military decrees with ouster clauses.

examples.q: A sitting governor cannot be sued for a civil wrong while in office. Which principle is limited and by what provision?
examples.a: Equality before the law is limited by section 308 of the 1999 Constitution, which confers immunity from civil and criminal proceedings on the President, Vice-President, Governors and Deputy Governors during their tenure.

modules.title: Separation of Powers
modules.html:
Separation of powers requires that the three functions of government — legislative, executive and judicial — be exercised by three separate sets of persons and bodies, so that no one organ becomes tyrannical. Montesquieu argued that “when the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person… there can be no liberty.”

Complete separation is impossible; what modern constitutions adopt is separation plus checks and balances:

Checking organCheck exercisedOn whom
LegislatureImpeachment; approval of appointments and budgets; override of veto; oversight and investigation.Executive and judiciary
ExecutiveVeto of bills; appointment of judges (subject to confirmation); prerogative of mercy.Legislature and judiciary
JudiciaryJudicial review; declaring laws or acts unconstitutional; interpreting the constitution.Legislature and executive

Merits: prevents dictatorship, protects liberty, promotes efficiency through specialisation, guarantees judicial independence. Demerits: can cause deadlock and delay, encourages friction between organs, and is difficult to apply strictly in a parliamentary system where the executive sits in the legislature.

examples.q: The National Assembly refuses to confirm a ministerial nominee. Which doctrine is at work?
examples.a: Checks and balances – the legislature restrains the executive's power of appointment through the requirement of Senate confirmation.

modules.title: Fundamental Human Rights
modules.html:
Human rights are the basic entitlements that belong to every person by virtue of being human. They are universal, inalienable and inherent. Chapter IV (sections 33–46) of Nigeria's 1999 Constitution guarantees:

  • Right to life (s.33)
  • Right to dignity of the human person — freedom from torture and slavery (s.34)
  • Right to personal liberty (s.35)
  • Right to fair hearing (s.36)
  • Right to private and family life (s.37)
  • Right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion (s.38)
  • Right to freedom of expression and the press (s.39)
  • Right to peaceful assembly and association (s.40)
  • Right to freedom of movement (s.41)
  • Right to freedom from discrimination (s.42)
  • Right to acquire and own immovable property anywhere in Nigeria (s.43) and protection from compulsory acquisition (s.44)

Rights are classified as civil and political (first generation, justiciable), economic, social and cultural (second generation, in Chapter II and non-justiciable in Nigeria), and collective or solidarity rights (third generation: development, peace, a clean environment).

Limitations: section 45 permits restrictions in the interest of defence, public safety, public order, public morality or public health, and to protect the rights of others. Rights may also be curtailed during a lawful state of emergency, though the right to life and freedom from torture enjoy strong protection.

examples.q: Can government lawfully ban a public procession? Explain.
examples.a: Yes, but only within limits. Section 40 guarantees peaceful assembly, yet section 45 allows a law reasonably justifiable in a democratic society to restrict it in the interest of public safety or order. A blanket, arbitrary ban would be unconstitutional.

modules.title: Enforcement of Rights and Judicial Independence
modules.html:
Section 46 gives any person who alleges that his rights are being or are likely to be infringed a direct right of access to a High Court. The Fundamental Rights (Enforcement Procedure) Rules provide a speedy procedure. Remedies include declarations, injunctions, damages and the prerogative writs — notably habeas corpus (production of a detained person), mandamus (compelling performance of a public duty), certiorari (quashing an unlawful decision) and prohibition.

Other safeguards: the National Human Rights Commission, the Public Complaints Commission (ombudsman), a free press, civil society organisations, and regional bodies such as the ECOWAS Community Court of Justice and the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights.

Independence of the judiciary is guaranteed by: security of tenure (judges removable only for misconduct through a prescribed procedure involving the National Judicial Council); salaries charged on the Consolidated Revenue Fund so they cannot be reduced to the judges' disadvantage; appointment on the recommendation of the National Judicial Council; immunity for judicial acts; and the contempt power.

examples.q: Which prerogative writ would you use for a person unlawfully detained by the police?
examples.a: Habeas corpus – an order directing the detaining authority to produce the detainee before the court and justify the detention, failing which the person must be released.

quiz.q: The rule of law was popularised by
quiz.solution: Dicey set out the doctrine in 1885.

quiz.q: Which is one of Dicey's pillars of the rule of law?
quiz.solution: Equality before the law is the second pillar.

quiz.q: Section 308 of the 1999 Constitution provides for
quiz.solution: It grants immunity to the President, VP, Governors and their deputies.

quiz.solution: Habeas corpus tests the legality of detention.

quiz.q: An order compelling a public officer to perform a duty is
quiz.solution: Mandamus commands performance of a public duty.

quiz.q: Section 45 of the 1999 Constitution provides for
options: Restriction of certain rights in the public interest
quiz.solution: It permits derogation on grounds such as public order and safety.

quiz.q: Security of tenure for judges is designed to ensure
quiz.solution: Judges must decide without fear of removal.

quiz.q: Which body recommends the appointment and discipline of judges in Nigeria?
quiz.solution: The NJC handles judicial appointments and discipline.

quiz.q: A demerit of strict separation of powers is
quiz.solution: Rival organs may frustrate one another.

quiz.solution: Solidarity or collective rights are third generation.
